For years, the Brennan Center has collected research showing that voter fraud is extraordinarily rare (http://www.brennancenter.org/analysis/debunking-voter-fraud-myth). Below is a review of developments and the literature on one subset of voter fraud claims - the allegation that ineligible noncitizens are voting in large numbers.
In 2024, a few elected state officials claim to have found people suspected of being noncitizens registered to vote. Some of them have already admitted (https://www.sos.alabama.gov/newsroom/secretary-state-wes-allen-implements-process-remove-noncitizens-registered-vote-alabama) that these searches likely include naturalized citizens. We do not have enough information yet to fully evaluate these claims. But, as set forth below, every time a state has conducted such investigations in the past, the result has been the same: actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.
Comprehensive Studies Have Found that Noncitizen Voting Is Vanishingly Rare
Rutgers University political scientist Lorraine C. Minnite has studied voter fraud allegations for more than a decade. She has concluded that voter fraud, including noncitizen voting, is "extremely rare." In one analysis (http://www.projectvote.org/wp-content/uploads/2007/03/Politics_of_Voter_Fraud_Final.pdf) of the first three years of a Justice Department initiative to uncover voter fraud ending in 2005, she found that there were only 14 convictions of noncitizens for voting.
In another study (https://www.amazon.com/Myth-Voter-Fraud-Lorraine-Minnite/dp/0801448484), Minnite examined all complaints of voter misconduct received by the California and Oregon secretaries of state for more than a decade. California received a total of 28 complaints of noncitizen voting, and Oregon, five. Out of that total, there were only four convictions.
In 2007, the Brennan Center conducted a nationwide survey (http://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legacy/The%20Truth%20About%20Voter%20Fraud.pdf) of a decade of news accounts and other complaints of noncitizen voting. The results showed that allegations of noncitizen voting that prove unfounded are far more common than allegations that turn out to be true. Some of the exaggerated or baseless allegations highlighted in that study include: A 2005 investigation into 1,668 Washington residents with "foreign-sounding names" which turned up no noncitizens; a 2000 investigation into 553 Hawaiians alleged to be improperly registered noncitizens, but none of whom had voted, and 2001 investigation in Milwaukee of 370,000 voting records that found four potential instances of naturalized persons voting before their naturalization date. Even if one accepts all of the allegations of noncitizen voting as true, noncitizens voters would have accounted for between .0002 percent and .017 percent of the votes in the relevant jurisdiction.
In 2015, three researches thoroughly debunked (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261379415001420?fr=RR-2&ref=pdf_download&rr=8845d244e8ea8c2d) the conclusions of a 2014 study by Jesse Richman claiming that 6.4 and 2.2 percent of noncitizens voted in the 2008 and 2010 elections, respectively. One of the authors of the study condemning Richman's work said of the refuted study: "As a member of the team that produces the datasets upon which that study was based . . . I can say unequivocally that this research is not only wrong, it is irresponsible social science and should never have been published in the first place." In 2020, the conservative Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) also rebuked the 2014 study. And in 2023, even Richman himself submitted an expert report for a case, analyzing the Arizona voter file and DMV files, and finding that only 1,934 voters (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/03/06/truth-about-noncitizen-voting-federal-elections/) had records that indicated they were not citizens at the time they registered or after registering to vote. Assuming the finding is true, the number amounts to .04 percent of the entire Arizona voter file of 4 million, a small fraction of the number of noncitizens he claimed had voted in his original study.
In 2016, the Brennan Center conducted a national survey of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally. Across these jurisdictions, election officials who oversaw the tabulation of 23.5 million votes in the 2016 election referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution. That is .0001 percent of votes case during that election.
State Investigations Have Uncovered Almost No Instances of Noncitizen Voting
A 2010 survey (http://ceimn.org/files/Facts%20about%20Ineligible%20Voting%20and%20Voter%20Fraud%20in%20Minnesota_with%20appendix.pdf) of Minnesota county attorneys found that, in the 18 months following the 2008 election, only nine incidents of possible noncitizen voting had been investigated out of 2.9 million ballots cast. None of these nine incidents resulted in a conviction.
New Mexico's secretary of state reviewed (http://nmpolitics.net/Documents/SOSVoterFileReport.pdf) that state's list of 1.2 million voters in 2011. The secretary of state's office only referred nine individuals to the state attorney general for investigation about their citizenship status.
In 2012, the Florida secretary of state reviewed a list of 180,000 potential noncitizens that the office set out to purge (http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-na-pol-noncitizen-voters-20161025-snap-story.html) at the request of the governor. After all the errors on that list were uncovered, only 85 names were removed from the rolls as alleged noncitizens, and only one (http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/08/31/josef-sever-canadian-voter-fraudflorida_n_1846662.html) person was convicted of fraud.
In 2012, after Michigan's secretary of state claimed (http://www.michigan.gov/sos/0,4670,7-127--286465--,00.html) that as many as 4,000 noncitizens were registered to vote, a review of the list resulted in only 10 people being referred (http://www.michigan.gov/sos/0,4670,7-127--317582--rss,00.html) to the state attorney general for further investigation because they had voted.
Also in 2012, Colorado's secretary of state identified (http://www.denverpost.com/2012/09/07/gessler-identifies-35-non-citizens-who-voted-but-holds-off-on-rule-making/) just 35 individuals on the rolls who were allegedly noncitizens and had voted. The investigation followed the secretary's original claim (https://www.brennancenter.org/blog/smoke-and-mirrors-alleged-non-citizen-voting-nm-and-co) that 11,805 noncitizens were registered to vote.
In a 2013 letter (http://www.ncleg.net/documentsites/committees/JointAppropriationsGeneralGovernment/2013%20Session/03-07-13%20Meeting/sbe_GA_response_with_attachments.pdf) to the North Carolina General Assembly, the executive director of the Board of Elections detailed every case of potential voter fraud in the state from 2002 to 2012. In those years, the Board of Elections referred 58 cases of potential noncitizen voting to prosecutors for further investigation. Considering that 19.5 million votes were cast in that time and assuming every allegation were true, noncitizen votes would have amounted to .0003 percent of the total.
In a check of the registration rolls in 2013 and 2015, Ohio's secretary of state concluded (http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/local/2015/03/12/husted-voting.html) that 44 noncitizens voted in at least one election dating back to 2000. By way of reference, there were 3.26 million ballots cast in Ohio in 2015 alone. "None of these affected the outcome of an election," Ohio Secretary of State John Husted told the Columbus Dispatch (http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/local/2015/03/12/husted-voting.html).
Iowa spent $250,000 (http://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/opinion/editorials/2014/05/16/matt-schultz-crusade-heavy-cost-light-vote-fraud/9157749/) from 2012 to 2014 looking into (http://publications.iowa.gov/16874/1/DCI%20Voter%20Fraud%20Report%205-8-14.pdf) potential noncitizen voters. It started with 3,000 individuals registered to vote who had at some point identified as noncitizens. That led to investigations of 147 individuals who had cast ballots, many of whom were discovered to be citizens. After two years of investigation, county attorneys brought charges against just 10 alleged noncitizens.
The Nevada secretary of state conducted a statewide audit (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/Home/Components/News/News/2229/309?backlist=%2fsos.) of voter rolls in 2016 and identified a mere three noncitizens who had registered and voted in the 2016 election. Considering that more than 1.1 million ballots were cast in Nevada for that election, noncitizen votes amounted to .0003 percent of the total.
Also in 2016, North Carolina State Board of Elections announced that 41 noncitizens cast ballots in the 2016 election. The U.S. Department of Justice charged 19 foreign nationals (https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/24/us/north-carolina-illegal-voters.html) with voting illegally in 2016 nationwide, which would have amounted to .0003 of the total ballots cast in North Carolina that election.
In 2017, the Ohio secretary of state announced (https://www.daytondailynews.com/news/state-more-than-100-non-citizens-have-voted-ohio/kLDaZOPtJBvlx1JNEWt1DJ/) that 126 noncitizens had cast a ballot since 2013, including 82 found in 2017 who the secretary referred to law enforcement for further investigation. Assuming the truth of allegations, even if all those votes occurred in the same year, noncitizen votes would have amounted to .0015 percent of the roughly 8 million people (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/election-results-and-data/historical-election-comparisons/voter-turnout-in-general-elections/) who vote in Ohio each election.
In 2019, Texas flagged almost 100,000 voters (https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2019/05/28/texas-secretary-state-resigns-after-leading-botched-voter-purge-that-questioned-citizenship-almost-people/) on its voter rolls as possible noncitizens. A federal court blocked (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2019/02/28/judge-blocks-gop-effort-purge-voting-rolls-texas-saying-it-is-ham-handed-threatening/) then-acting Texas Secretary of State David Whitley from purging these voters, many of whom were actually naturalized citizens. The court called Whitley's efforts "a solution looking for a problem."
In 2020, after an investigation into alleged noncitizen voting, the Ohio secretary of state referred 104 cases of alleged noncitizen voter registration and 13 cases of alleged noncitizen voting for prosecution. Assuming the truth of the latter figure, noncitizen ballots cast would have amounted to .00016 percent of the ballots cast during the primary and general that year. In contextualizing the finding, Ohio's own secretary of state admitted that "voter fraud is exceedingly rare (https://www.toledoblade.com/local/politics/2021/07/12/13-suspected-non-citizens-voted-in-2020-ohio-elections/stories/20210712127)."
In 2022, the Georgia secretary of state's office conducted a citizenship review (https://sos.ga.gov/news/citizenship-audit-finds-1634-noncitizens-attempted-register-vote) of the state's voter rolls and found that it could not verify the citizenship of 1,634 voter registration applicants but that the state's registration procedures screened the applicants, and none had actually voted.
Nationwide Surveys by Journalists Found that Noncitizen Voting Is Practically Nonexistent
After the 2016 election, the New York Times surveyed (http://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/18/us/voter-fraud.html?_r=0) election and law enforcement officials in 49 states and the District of Columbia. It learned of two possible instances of noncitizens voting out of 137.7 million voters nationwide.
The Washington Post also did a survey (https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/12/01/0-000002-percent-of-all-the-ballots-cast-in-the-2016-election-were-fraudulent/?utm_term=.37e784f03e2e) after the 2016 election. It compiled reports from the Nexis database. In all, the Post found four demonstrated cases of any type of voter fraud, and no instances of noncitizens voting.
News21, an investigative reporting project based at Arizona State University, reviewed (https://news.asu.edu/content/news21-students-investigate-voting-rights) all reported instances of voter fraud from 2000 to 2012. It found 56 cases of alleged noncitizen voting. Even assuming all of these allegations are true and that all of these purported noncitizens voted in 2016, it would total approximately .00004 percent of all ballots cast.
Past Claims of Noncitizen Voting by Public Entities and Personalities Have Been Disproved
In 2016 and 2017, the Public Interest Legal Foundation (PILF), a conservative legal organization, published two reports purporting to show (https://www.huffpost.com/entry/j-christian-adams-pilf-settlement_n_5d309002e4b0419fd3298ee6) that thousands of noncitizens were registered to vote in Virginia. Blog Post · October 29, 2026
Does California Have a Problem with Noncitizen Voting?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
The Trump administration is suing California to block votes from over 20,000 registered voters (https://www.kbtx.com/2026/10/28/special-master-could-evaluate-justice-departments-claims-noncitizens-california-voter-rolls/) who the administration alleges are not citizens. It has followed up this suit with specific legal action (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/us/politics/doj-california-voting-crimes-trump-midterms.html) against 28 people from the broader list. The administration argues that the state, in refusing to sequester the ballots, is obstructing efforts to ensure election integrity. Where does the administration’s claim come from? And does California have a noncitizen voting problem?
California’s demography alone makes it a target for concerns about noncitizen voting, since it has more noncitizens than any other state (12.7%). Moreover, while California does require identification when registering to vote, it does so largely to establish name and residence, not citizenship. Many of the permissible forms of ID (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) are items noncitizens can just as easily possess.
Citizenship is verified not with ID but by asking the prospective voter to attest to citizenship, under penalty of perjury. California is not alone in this approach. All but 12 states verify citizenship with attestation (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/requiring-documentary-proof-of-citizenship), and 8 of those 12 exceptions started requiring documentation only in 2024 or later. At the other end of the spectrum, North Dakota does not have voter registration at all.
California in recent years has adopted several reforms (https://www.ppic.org/publication/do-registration-reforms-add-new-voters-or-keep-californians-registered/) to encourage and facilitate voter registration, and these may have contributed to speculation about noncitizen registrations. The state now has automatic voter registration for those visiting the Department of Motor Vehicles for a standard license or state ID transaction. Before customers can complete their transaction, the touch screen at the DMV requires them to say if they want to register and are a citizen. The state also has an online registration platform that walks users through the standard questions and gets them registered. Together these two methods now account for about six in ten recent registrations. (It is also still possible to register with a paper form, available at post offices, public libraries, county election offices, and the DMV.)
Any of these methods of registration have a deadline of at least 15 days before the election. However, California also has “conditional” voter registration, which allows registration and voting at in-person voting sites after the 15-day voter registration deadline. These ballots are sequestered and are not counted until they can be validated.
These reforms—especially automatic voter registration—have greatly increased the volume of registrations. Since each transaction carries some potential for error, the total number of errors may grow as a result. Otherwise, none of these new systems adds any particular risk for noncitizen registration that did not already exist with paper forms.
In fact, volume alone may be an important driver of concerns about noncitizen voting. Registration files have millions of records, and the errors inherent to any big database. There are always at least a few noncitizens who end up registered and voting, because they either intended to break the rules or found them confusing, or because the state made a mistake. But that does not make noncitizen voting common.
The administration’s 20,000-person list has been culled from a larger list of 191,000 people (https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/17/dhs-secretary-markwayne-mullin-sends-letters-secretaries-state-warning-about-non). This much higher number—troubling if true—amounts to about 0.8% of California’s active registered voter list. Past efforts in other states to identify noncitizen voters often started with numbers in the thousands or even tens of thousands and usually ended up (https://www.denverpost.com/2012/09/15/noncitizen-voters-idd-fraction-of-those-first-alleged-by-gessler/) with counts (https://www.texastribune.org/2019/02/08/texas-ken-paxton-voter-fraud-non-citizens-not-prosecuted/) of a few hundred (https://www.foxnews.com/politics/florida-officials-find-198-non-citizens-on-voter-rolls-after-extensive-search.amp) at most, with almost no criminal convictions (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/15/us/politics/noncitizen-voting-data.html). The administration’s prosecution of 28 people from an original list of 191,000 fits with this historical pattern.
The administration has not made public the methodology behind either the list of 191,000 or the smaller one with 20,000. A parallel effort through the Census Bureau to identify noncitizen voters from 2020 (https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2026/dir/noncitizen-voting-in-the-2020-election.pdf) may offer some insight: the matching algorithm used in that effort has an error rate many times larger than the number of noncitizen voters that were found, making each identified record more likely to be a mistake (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/john-abowd-cornell_noncitizen-voting-in-the-2020-election-a-share-7496379718938566656-EbBE/).
Noncitizen voters should be identified, and prosecuted when appropriate. But the evidentiary bar for removing records from the rolls should be high to avoid disenfranchising legitimate voters.

Vote By Mail
Vote By Mail
Choose Language
English español
County elections officials mail vote-by-mail ballots to all active registered voters. If you believe you are already registered, you can verify your registration online with our "My Voter Status (https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/)" tool. If you are not already registered, you can register online at RegisterToVote.ca.gov (http://registertovote.ca.gov/).
Voting By Mail
Any registered voter may vote using a vote-by-mail ballot instead of going to the polls on Election Day.
After you have voted, insert your ballot in the envelope provided, making sure you complete all required information on the envelope.
You may return your voted ballot by
By drop box
Drop off your completed ballot in the return envelope at a secure official drop box in your county at any time between October 5 through the close of polls on November 3.
In person
Drop your completed ballot in the return envelope off at a secure drop box, polling place, vote center, or county elections office by 8:00 p.m. on November 3. Voting locations will be available in all counties before Election Day. Voting locations offer voter registration, replacement ballots, accessible voting machines, and language assistance.
By mail
Return your ballot by mail as soon as you receive it. Mailed ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received not later than 7 days after Election Day. To ensure your ballot is postmarked by Election Day make sure to mail it at least five days before Election Day, November 3, 2026. If mailing on Election Day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a United States Post Office.
Authorizing someone to return the ballot on your behalf.
Anyone may return your ballot for you, as long as they do not get paid on a per ballot basis.
When your vote-by-mail ballot is received by your county elections official (http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/county-elections-offices/), your signature on the return envelope will be compared to the signature(s) in your voter registration record. To preserve the secrecy of your ballot, the ballot will then be separated from the return envelope, and then it will be tallied.
All valid vote-by-mail ballots are counted in every election in California, regardless of the outcome or closeness of any race. For additional information on how and when ballots are verified and tabulated, please visit our description of how the official canvass of the vote (http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/official-canvass/) is completed.
For more information on voting by mail, see our "Vote-by-Mail Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/vbm-faq.pdf)" document.
Voting for the First Time
When you registered to vote, you were asked to fill in your driver license number, California identification number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. If you are a first-time voter in a federal election and did not include this information when you registered, send a photocopy of some personal identification to your county elections official before the election.
A copy of a recent utility bill, the county Voter Information Guide you received from your county elections office, or another document sent to you by a government agency are examples of acceptable forms of identification. Other examples include your passport, driver license, official California identification card, or student identification card.
If your identity cannot be verified, then your Vote-by-Mail ballot return envelope will not be opened.
For more information on identification to use when you vote for the first time, check the complete list of acceptable forms of identification (PDF) (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) or call the Secretary of State's toll-free voter hotline at (800) 345-VOTE (8683).
Status of your Vote-By-Mail Ballot
California Elections Code section 3017(c) requires county elections officials to establish procedures to track and confirm the receipt of voted vote-by-mail ballots and to make this information available by means of an online access system using the county's elections division web site or via a toll-free telephone number.
You may also check the status of your ballot by visiting, "My Voter Status (https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/)."
Where's My Ballot
The California Secretary of State is now offering Where's My Ballot? -a new way for voters to track and receive notiﬁcations on the status of their vote-by-mail ballot. Powered by BallotTrax, Where's My Ballot? lets voters know where their ballot is, and its status, every step of the way.
A voter who has signed up will receive notices via email, text, or voice message from the county elections official regarding the status of the voter's vote-by-mail ballot including:
When the ballot has been delivered
The date that the voter's ballot is expected to be delivered to the voter
If the voter's ballot is returned as undeliverable to the county elections official by the USPS
When the voter's completed ballot has been received by the county
Whether the voter's completed ballot has been accepted or a reason why the ballot could not be accepted and instructions of steps the voter can take in order to have the ballot accepted
The deadline for the voter to return his or her ballot if the county has not received a voter's completed ballot by specified dates as determined by the county elections official
Sign-up at WheresMyBallot.sos.ca.gov (https://california.ballottrax.net/voter/) to receive automatic email, SMS (text), or voice call notiﬁcations about your ballot.
Where's My Ballot? is available in all 58 California counties.
California Replacement Ballot Application
A voter who did not receive their vote-by-mail ballot, or lost or destroyed their original ballot, may apply for a replacement ballot. Only the registered voter themself may request a replacement ballot.
The application should be returned to their local county elections office. A voter may also request a replacement ballot from their county elections office by phone, email, fax, or other electronic means.

Missing or Noncomparable Signature on Your Vote-by-Mail Ballot Return Envelope
Common issues with vote-by-mail or provisional ballot return envelopes include:
Missing Signature : You may have forgotten to sign your vote-by-mail ballot return envelope.
Signature Doesn't Compare : The signature doesn't compare with the one on file with the elections official.
If there's an issue with the signature, your county elections office will notify you via mail, phone, email, or through the Secretary of State's "Where's My Ballot? (https://california.ballottrax.net/voter/)" tool. To fix it, follow the instructions provided by your county, which will include completing a form to verify your signature. Be sure to submit the form properly to ensure your vote is counted. For more information, see our How to Fix a Missing or Noncomparable Signature on Your Vote-by-Mail Ballot Return Envelope (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2025-special/trusted-info-missing-signature.pdf) document.
Military & Overseas Vote-By-Mail Voting
As a military or overseas voter, in order to receive your election materials and vote when you are absent from your county while serving and/or living overseas, you need to be registered as a military or overseas voter by completing the California Online Voter Registration (COVR) application (https://registertovote.ca.gov/) or by completing the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA). The FPCA is available from the Federal Voting Assistance Program (http://www.fvap.gov/).
For additional information, please visit our Military and Overseas Voting Information (http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/military-overseas-voters/) section.
Best Practices for Vote-By-Mail Envelope Design
The Center for Civic Design has consulted with the United States Postal Service (USPS) to complete a review of the universal vote-by-mail envelope package that was first launched in 2018. During that consultation, the Center for Civic Design identified several changes to better meet service guidelines and ensure that vote by mail ballots are successfully delivered. Utilizing these uniform guidelines can assist in statewide voter education efforts, ensure voters receive their materials timely, and aid voters in understanding the materials that are sent to them. As many voters will experience voting by mail for the first time, the Secretary of State's office encourages counties to utilize the resources provided by the Center for Civic Design to assist in a successful rollout of increased vote-by-mail voting.
The Center for Civic Design has provided updated USPS templates (PDF) (https://civicdesign.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/VAH-USPSrules-2020-0618.pdf), InDesign templates of the outgoing (ZIP) (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vote-by-mail/vbm-outgoing-envelope.zip) and return (ZIP) (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vote-by-mail/vbm-return-envelope.zip) envelopes, and an updated informational USPS flyer (PDF) (https://civicdesign.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/USPS-Info-Flyer_TEMPLATE-2020-0328-1.pdf) for counties to use in implementing this updated universal design. They have also provided sample voter information inserts (PDF) (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vote-by-mail/pdf/sample-inserts.pdf) to use in county vote-by-mail packages and an updated color palette (PDF) (https://civicdesign.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Oxide-CCD-VBM-Envelope-Color-Palette-Update-02.pdf). You may find these updated templates and more by visiting the Center for Civic Design's (https://civicdesign.org/fieldguides/104-designing-vote-at-home-envelopes/) website.

**Considering voter ID requirements**

I'm trying to figure out if the envelope for mail ballots must show the identification number. The text indicates that each voter's ID type needs to be noted in their registration record and on the envelope. However, it doesn't explicitly say the full ID number is needed, just the type. They must write the last four digits instead. It seems like the risk of exposing personal details is lower when only partial information is shared.**Analyzing ballot rejection claims**

The YES side claims over 100,000 mail ballots were rejected in 2024 due to signature mismatches. However, I see the official figures show 71,381 for mismatched signatures and an additional 13,356 for missing signatures, totaling 84,737, which is still under 100,000. The campaign clarified their figure, but there seems to be a discrepancy. It’s essential to identify if they were combining the 2024 primary and general elections, which might push the number closer to 100,000.**Assessing ballot rejection claims**

The claim of "over 100,000 ballots rejected in 2024 due to signature mismatches" seems to conflict with the official figure of 71,381 mismatches. It's possible that the total includes other types of rejections as well. The official ballot guide notes nearly 100,000 rejected, but I wonder if this statement is material. Accurate data from official sources should be the priority. I need to gather more information and independent studies on voter ID impacts, as findings vary and it's crucial to represent this accurately.**Evaluating ID laws and turnout effects**

Laws around voter ID might create some barriers, but the effects on turnout aren't consistently observed. This could be due to factors like the availability of free IDs, outreach efforts, and political mobilization at the sample level. In California, for instance, providing free IDs is supposed to lower these barriers, so I need to consider how these factors influence actual voter participation. It's crucial to analyze real-world implications of these policies effectively.

# Judge rejects challenge to California attorney general’s description of voter ID measure
A state judge Thursday rejected a challenge to how California Atty.
Gen. Rob Bonta’s office summarized a strict new voter ID measure on November ballots — ruling that the summary language accurately describes the measure’s effects were it to pass.
Another judge dealt the backers of the measure a second loss by tentatively finding that their description of the measure, submitted for the official state voter’s guide, was misleading.
They had claimed that Proposition 39 would make voting easier.
In the first case, Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the label, title and summary of the certified ballot measure accurately describe Proposition 39 as a measure that “prohibits citizens from voting” — language the measure’s backers specifically objected to — unless they provide a government-issued ID.
According to minutes from a Thursday hearing on the matter, Rockwell concluded that, to the extent the measure’s backers object to that language, they are objecting to “the provisions of the measure itself.”
Rockwell rejected the argument put forth by the measure’s backers that it would not prevent people without ID from voting, only their votes from being counted — a distinction the judge found lacking.

Yes, "Voter ID laws" are on the California ballot: Proposition 39's rules, costs, and court fights
Proposition 39 would make California the latest state to require ID to vote, replacing signature checks on 13 million mail ballots with a four-digit ID match. Here is how voting works today, exactly what the measure changes, what it would cost, and who is paying for each side.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 08, 2026

California voter ID rules would change for every in-person and mail voter under Proposition 39 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
Proposition 39 asks California voters to write a voter identification requirement into the state Constitution. If it passes, every voter would present government-issued identification to vote in person, and every mail voter, which in November 2024 meant about 13 million of the 16 million who voted, would write the last four digits of a designated ID number on the ballot envelope, where today they sign their name. The measure, placed on the ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) by petition and sponsored by Reform California's Carl DeMaio, is one of the 14 statewide propositions in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it is the one whose polling the campaigns dispute most.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The measure is short, about 400 words of operative text, and much of the argument around it concerns what those words leave out. This explainer sets out how voting in California works now, what Prop 39's text actually requires, what the Legislative Analyst says it would cost, how two Sacramento judges ruled on the campaigns' language in August, and who is funding each side.
Proposition 39 is changing the verification step for in-person and mail voting in California from a signature to a government-issued identification number, as the measure's text and the Elections Code show in October 2026.
Proposition 39 adds one section to the Constitution with three requirements
The measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution. Its findings say the purpose is "to deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote" and "to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by requiring proof of identity to vote." The operative provisions are three.
First, citizenship verification: the Secretary of State and county elections officials "shall use best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data, and shall annually report what percentage of each county's voter rolls have been citizenship-verified."
Second, identification at the ballot: "Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration." The type of ID each voter designates must be recorded in their registration and printed on their mail-ballot envelope. Officials "shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section." The measure's only definition of acceptable ID is that it "means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter's identity," and it requires the state to provide "at no charge, a voter ID card" to any eligible voter who asks.
Third, enforcement: the section is "self-executing," the Legislature "shall also promptly enact laws to implement" it, citizens may seek judicial review of any county's compliance, and in every odd-numbered year the State Auditor must audit the state and every county and report publicly.
The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm) draws out a consequence the text implies but does not spell out: the measure "invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter's registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver's license number on envelope, their ballot would not count)." Nothing in the measure describes what happens next. There is no notice-and-cure provision of the kind that exists today for signature mismatches, and no list of which documents qualify. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) says the Legislature "would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters."
Voting in California today runs on signatures, not identification
The Secretary of State's own guidance (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/what-bring) to voters begins: "In most cases, a California voter is not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot." Under Elections Code section 14216 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216), an in-person voter states their name and address, the poll worker finds them in the roster, and the voter signs. # What to know about California's Proposition 39 ahead of general election
One of the highest-profile measures on California's November ballot is Proposition 39, which would require voters to show a government-issued ID to vote.
Supporters say the measure would strengthen public confidence in California's elections, while opponents argue it would create new barriers to voting.
Support for the measure has raised more than $36 million, while opposition has raised more than $27 million, according to the California Secretary of State.
...
## What the voter ID initiative would do
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would:
- Require voters casting a ballot by mail to provide a government-issued ID number.
- Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.

California has two methods to verify the results of each election.
Counties must use one or both to certify the results of every election.

# Risk-Limiting Audits
A risk-limiting audit is a method of ensuring that election results match voter selections reflected on paper ballots.
For California counties that choose to conduct a risk-limiting audit, using statistical sampling techniques, elections officials review a sample of ballots cast in an election to confirm that the reported results tabulated by the voting system are accurate.
Additional ballots may be reviewed as necessary until the results of the election are confirmed to a certain degree of confidence.
In California, when a risk-limiting audit is used, it must confirm that the election results reported by the voting system are 95% likely to be accurate.
Unlike the post-election 1% manual tally traditionally used to confirm election results in California, under a risk-limiting audit every ballot cast in the election—regardless of which precinct it was cast in—has an equal chance of being audited.

Proposition 39 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-39) would change how Californians verify their identities when voting, replacing signature matching for mail-in ballots with government-issued identification numbers and requiring identification at polling places. Hoover Institution scholar Justin Grimmer examines the proposal, the safeguards already in place, and what research reveals about voter fraud and election security. He also addresses concerns that stricter identification requirements could discourage voting, explaining why studies suggest their effects on turnout and election outcomes are minimal. Grimmer also explores whether Proposition 39 could strengthen public trust in California's elections.
ABOUT THE SERIES
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.
Launching in advance of the 2026 election, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) will answer the questions Californians are already asking (from housing affordability and energy costs to education, public safety, state finances, and election administration) while also explaining how California government works and what the governor, Legislature, and ballot initiatives can and cannot change. More than an election resource, California Decides is intended to become Hoover’s permanent platform for California civic education: a trusted destination where voters, policymakers, journalists, educators, and community leaders can find clear, evidence-based explanations of the state’s most important challenges and the choices that will shape its future.

California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides)
Summary
A sound election system has to do two things simultaneously: Prevent voter fraud while ensuring that every eligible vote is counted. Proposition 39 is arguably an attempt to improve electoral confidence while minimizing negative effects on ballot access.
Proposition 39 requires that voters provide either state-issued identification to vote in person or the last four digits of a government-issued identification number to vote by mail-in ballot, similar to many other states. It also requires that elections officials publish regular eligibility audits of voter rolls. Lastly, it mandates that California create an alternate state ID card so that those who don’t have other forms of ID, like a driver’s license, are able to vote.
Given that over 80 percent of California voters make use of mail-in ballots, Proposition 39’s greatest impacts will be on mail-in voting rather than in-person voting. California’s recent shift to all-mail elections has vastly expanded the ease of voting and, as a result, voter participation. It also has opened up a new, more rewarding avenue for voter fraud. There is no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California. Yet instances of fraud have been uncovered, and the increase of mail-in voting has coincided with decreasing confidence in the honesty of elections.
Because California’s existing election systems already requires elections officials to contact voters—by mail, email, and phone—to “cure” their mail-in ballot of any deficiencies and allows voters twenty-two days after Election Day to do so, expanding identification requirements does not seem likely to substantially inhibit valid votes from being counted.
Realistically, there is an inherent trade-off between election legitimacy and making voting easy. This measure effectively asks voters whether increased legitimacy is worth making voting slightly more difficult.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The original title was “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” but this was changed by the California attorney general to “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification.” Ballot measure proponents challenged the new name as misleading, but the deputy attorney general argued that the title is only misleading if read in isolation. The Sacramento Superior Court ruled the changed title and summary were “sufficient.”
Measure’s own name: The California Voter ID Initiative (AG No. 25-0007A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: Voters must show government-issued ID to vote in person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number on their mail-in ballot envelopes. The state must offer a free voter ID card and conduct regular audits of voter rolls to verify eligibility and citizenship.
A vote NO means: California keeps its current system, which asks for no ID at the polls and verifies mail ballots by signature match.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0007A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0007 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-007)
1. What would it do?
More than two-thirds of states require a voter to provide identification to receive a ballot, and recent national polls by the Pew Research Center, Rasmussen Reports, and Gallup show that over 75 percent of US adults support photo ID requirements to vote. California is one of the remaining states that does not ask for any identification for in-person voting. Under this measure, anyone voting in person would have to present a government-issued ID to receive a ballot.
A similar requirement would apply to mail-in ballots. Under the measure, a mail-in voter would have to write the last four digits of a unique government-issued identification number (such as Social Security number, driver’s license number, or Voter ID card) on the ballot envelope. That number would be matched against the voter’s registration record before the ballot is counted.
For context, Minnesota already uses a similar system that requires a voter-specific identification number to verify mail-in ballots. To further ensure election integrity, Minnesota law also requires that absentee voters show their blank ballot to a witness (who must be a US citizen, notary, or public official) prior to the voter filling it out, and then requires that witness’s signature on the signature envelope certifying that the ballot was completed privately. Before the ballot is recorded at least two members of the absentee ballot board (either election officials or representatives of different political parties) review each signature envelope to ensure that it matches the voter’s name, address, signature, and voter identification number and has a witness signature.
Proposition 39 includes three more parts to facilitate voter identification and the validation of voter rolls. First, it requires the state to provide a free voter ID card on request, reducing the ballot access issues that can be caused by using a driver’s license as the default identification. Second, it requires the California Secretary of State’s office and county election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, use government data to verify citizenship attestations, and publicly report each year what share of the rolls has been citizenship-verified. Lastly, it is self-executing, such that every two years the California State Auditor’s Office must publish an audit of state and county election officials’ compliance. It also empowers any citizen to seek judicial review and remedy if they believe that state or county officials are not complying with the constitutional amendment.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0007A1, “California Voter ID Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf) (as amended August 7, 2025)
Key language: “Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration.”
What it amends:
Adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution, the article that governs voting. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot simply repeal it, and it directs the legislature to enact implementing laws and to provide for military and overseas voters consistent with federal law.
3. Who, What, Where, When, Why?
What would it change about voting?
It would require a government-issued ID for in-person voting or the provision of the last four digits of a government ID number for mail voting. It requires the state to provide a free state ID card on request. Lastly, it mandates that the state regularly verify the citizenship of registered voters and report the results of that audit.
Where would it take effect?
Statewide, in every election.
When would it take effect?
The measure is self-executing on passage, such that the legislature is directed to enact implementing laws, and the state auditor is directed to publish an audit of compliance by state and county election officials in every odd-numbered year.
Why add identification rules to the voting process?
The proponents’ stated goals for this measure are to promote public confidence in the electoral process and voting results by deterring and detecting fraud, confirming voter eligibility, and minimizing voter impersonation.
4. Trade-offs
The 2020 presidential election results were controversially challenged as being manipulated by widespread voter fraud—an allegation that was believed by three out of every eight voters. The extensive mail-in voting allowed due to COVID-19 pandemic concerns was blamed as part of this alleged fraud. However, documented cases of election fraud are rare, and the most rigorous review of the 2020 election did not find evidence to support claims of systematic fraud.
A more general issue is that voter fraud statistics only measure the fraud that we have been able to detect and, more importantly, the fraud that was perpetrated within the system as it previously existed. The next sections examine:
The ways that elections have substantially changed over the last fifty years, with major changes accelerating over the last decade
How these changes provide a rational argument for those concerned with voter fraud
How the changes, at least in part, seem to be linked to declining voter confidence in elections
The type of fraud inhibited by ID requirements for in-person voting—where one person impersonates another at the polling place—is the rarest documented form of voter fraud. This doesn’t make in-person voter identification unimportant, but in-person voter fraud is arguably the smallest part of the problem. The elephant in the room, so to speak, is the significant increase in mail-in voting.
In brief summary, California’s mail-in voting system verifies eligibility mainly through the voter’s own attestation that they are who they say they are and by matching their signature to a previous signature on record (see the California Decides FAQ: How Elections Are Run (https://www.hoover.org/research/how-elections-are-run) for additional information). The lack of a rigorous means to validate who specifically filled out the mail-in ballot—which is done in private, far away from the public view of voting centers—increases the potential for voter fraud. Furthermore, the lack of clearer voter identification mechanisms means that investigations into whether voter fraud occurred will struggle to definitively certify the lack of fraud. That validation gap is precisely the proponents’ argument for building a more complete verification infrastructure.
Changes to US Elections
US elections have seen major changes since states started expanding absentee mail-in voting in the 1970s. This, like early in-person voting, has led to large decreases in voting at public polling locations on Election Day. In the last two presidential elections, over 80 percent of Californians voted by mail.
At the national level:
In-person voting on Election Day has been steadily decreasing, from around 90 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 60 percent in 2016. That percentage dropped to 31 percent in 2020 and recovered slightly to 40 percent in 2024.
Meanwhile, absentee/mail-in voting has been steadily increasing, from around 8 percent of votes cast in the mid-1990s to 21 percent of votes cast in 2016. During the pandemic mail-in ballots surged to 43 percent of votes cast in 2020 and then returned to the previous trend, accounting for 29 percent of votes in 2024.
Early in-person voting has seen a similar upward trajectory, from 2–3 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 19 percent in 2016. The trend has accelerated faster than mail-in voting, with early in-person voting accounting for 26 percent of votes cast in 2020 and 31 percent of votes cast in 2024.
The shift away from in-person voting on Election Day seems to have increased voter anxiety about the electoral process, perhaps due to the reduced ability to identify fraud and therefore a perception that fraud would be easier to employ. Currently, eight states now practice all-mail elections (where every eligible voter receives a ballot by mail), twenty-nine more allow no-excuse absentee voting, and forty-seven allow some form of early in-person voting.
California was the first state to allow no-excuse absentee voting, starting in 1979. By 2012, a majority of California ballots were submitted by mail. Starting in 2018, the state allowed county elections officials to shift to an all-mail election, and the state itself adopted an all-mail ballot starting in 2020. This led to over 86 percent of ballots being cast by mail in 2020, followed by over 80 percent in 2024.
Concerns about Ballot Harvesting
In California, concerns about voter fraud have probably been exacerbated by legislation passed in 2016 that legalized unlimited third-party ballot collection, a practice that is more generally known as ballot harvesting. It allows any person to collect and submit any number of mail-in ballots, including paid campaign workers and volunteer advocates. The same year, other legislation enabled county election officials to mail every registered voter a ballot, expand early in-person voting, and create ballot drop box locations with 24/7 access.
In theory, the mail-in ballots should already be filled out and sealed when given to the ballot harvester, such that there’s little opportunity for the harvester to view or change the vote. There is no way to ensure this, but it’s also relevant to highlight that changing another person’s ballot (or filling it out without their approval) has never been legal and is the most fundamental form of voter fraud.
Opponents of ballot harvesting argue that the practice breaks the intrinsic chain of custody for mail-in ballots—from the voter to US Postal Service staff to elections officials—and therefore impugns the integrity of such ballots. Proponents argue that it enables greater voter participation. Both things can be simultaneously true: Many voters likely find it easier to vote, and unscrupulous political agents also have greater ability to practice fraud (regardless of whether they have actually exercised that ability to date or have done so in statistically measurable ways).
By law, the ballot harvester is required to provide their name and signature on the ballot return envelope. However, there currently doesn’t seem to be any way to validate that ballot harvesters are adhering to this requirement, because there’s nothing that distinguishes a ballot submitted by a ballot harvester from one submitted by the voter. The current system effectively places ballot harvesters on the honor system to provide that information on each ballot they submit via mail or ballot drop box, because without providing that information it appears to the elections officials that the voter submitted the ballot themselves.
Decreasing Voter Confidence and Perceived Election Honesty
At the national level, voters’ confidence in whether their own vote is counted correctly is generally high, but there is reduced confidence in whether national voting in general is counted correctly. There is also clearly declining confidence in the general honesty of elections.
It’s important to note that while voter confidence has indeed decreased over recent decades, in the short run a major part of this sentiment seems to be driven by whether a voter’s preferred candidate won the election (called the winner-loser effect). This can be particularly seen in the 2024 election, when Republican-leaning voters went into the election with very low confidence in whether their vote would be counted and then reported greater confidence in US elections following President Trump’s victory. Democratic-leaning voters shifted in the opposite direction, but the size of the change was not as substantial.
5. Conclusion
Passage of Proposition 39 would bring California into line with most other states. Voter ID requirements receive broad, bipartisan support—more than 75 percent of voters support requiring a photo ID to vote—and the ballot measure addresses a real gap in how the state verifies voter eligibility.
The trade-off for greater electoral confidence is that voter ID requirements can cause some eligible ballots to be rejected for honest mistakes. However, the legislature can effectively solve this problem by employing a system similar to that which California already uses, which requires election officials to contact voters to rectify problems with the identification the voter submitted and provides twenty-two days after Election Day to do so.
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.
